articles.title: I got tired of typing "do 1 and 3, skip 2" to Claude Code, so I built an approve/reject board
articles.summary: You ask Claude Code for ten improvements to your project. It answers with a tidy numbered list. Then the real work starts: you scroll, you type "do 1 and 3, skip 2 because we tried that, maybe 5 later," and you hope the agent maps your sentence back to the right items. Next week, in a new session, it proposes number 2 again. So I built ar-board, a Claude Code plugin that turns the list into cards on a local page. You judge each card with one key (approve, reject, or maybe) and a short reason. The agent gets back an exact list of what you approved, and your reasons go into a preferences file it reads before it proposes anything next time. One Python file, standard library only, MIT licensed. The panel opens in English, and an EN/PT toggle in its header switches it to Portuguese. The cards are in whatever language you and the agent are using. You can try a sketch of the board in your browser before installing. The short version I checked 34 live apps that their makers shared publicly on X between Oct 20 and Oct 24, 2026. articles.title: A pre-flight checklist before domain continued pre-training
articles.summary: Your team picked an open weight checkpoint and a corpus. The tempting move is to schedule GPUs and iterate on the mix later. Joel Hron at Thomson Reuters and Fergal Reid at Intercom both describe training as staged pipelines where evaluation sits beside the data, and Hron treats retained capabilities as an explicit objective. I'd treat the run as blocked until you can answer the questions below. What training stage are you actually running? Most product teams are not pretraining from scratch. They adapt a base model in layers. Continued pre-training adds more unlabeled domain text on top of an existing checkpoint. Supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization teach labeled behavior. Agentic reinforcement learning teaches tool use inside a harness. articles.title: OpenAI Moderation API and GPT-4o-mini Chat Completions: JSON Schema Text Triage
articles.summary: Short answer: treat text moderation as a queue contract, not a prompt trick. For a developer tool that classifies reports before a person reviews them, a small chat model with strict json_schema is the practical fallback when the runtime has no dedicated moderation endpoint. Keep the result narrow: { "is_safe": boolean, "reason": string }. Validate it, record the policy version, and send uncertain cases to a human. The main trade is governance. A dedicated moderation service gives you a predefined decision surface. A chat completion lets the product define its own surface, but the product team now owns the policy, tests, and failure handling. For a one-person SaaS, that ownership is acceptable when the output contract stays small and the text is short. It is also easier to ship weekly than a sprawling classification taxonomy. articles.title: Claude Code hooks for teams: four hooks worth committing to your repo
articles.summary: Most teams start shaping Claude Code with instructions: a CLAUDE.md file that says "run the formatter," "never edit the lockfile," "use our logger." That works most of the time. But an instruction is something the model chooses to follow. On a long session, or a busy day, it sometimes doesn't. Hooks close that gap. A hook is a shell command that Claude Code runs automatically at a fixed point, such as after every file edit or before every command. It runs every time, whether or not the model remembers the rule. For a team, that changes what you can promise. "The agent should format its code" becomes "the agent's code is always formatted." Where team hooks live Hooks go in the same settings files as permissions. For a team, the one that matters is .claude/settings.json in the repository, committed like any other config. articles.title: OpenStripe supports open-set identification and spatial stripe profiling in wild Amur tigers
articles.summary: Non-invasive camera-trap monitoring of endangered wildlife requires open-set individual identification---grouping field images into identities without predefined classes or a known population size---yet pose deformation and cluttered backgrounds complicate image comparison. Here, we present OpenStripe, a multi-agent framework that reconstructs canonical two-dimensional (2D) tiger torso patterns and encodes four interpretable local stripe structures: breakpoints, bifurcations, irregular structures, and round structures. We evaluated OpenStripe on 100 camera-trap records from 28 wild Amur tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), representing nearly one-third of the documented population in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park. Combining all four complementary structures enabled automatic identity grouping with 0.90 matched accuracy and a 0.85 adjusted Rand index (ARI), outperforming 49 baseline configurations under the same backend (up to 0.43 accuracy and 0.14 ARI). articles.title: What a LongMemEval Score Does and Doesn't Tell You About Memory for Coding Agents
articles.summary: The LongMemEval benchmark is a public test of long-term memory in chat assistants. It has 500 hand-written questions, and each one sits on top of a long history of past chat sessions between a user and an assistant. To answer a question, a system has to find the right facts in that history and reason over them. The facts may be spread across sessions, may have changed over time, or may not exist at all. The test was published in 2024 and comes in two common sizes. LongMemEval-S gives each question a history of roughly 115,000 tokens. LongMemEval-M uses far larger histories, well beyond what fits in any model's context window. It has become the standard way to compare memory systems for AI assistants. At Open Agentic Brain & Memory (OpenAB), we report a LongMemEval score too. The OpenAB project page lists 94.2% on LongMemEval-S while reading 75% fewer tokens, measured over all 500 questions with a Claude reader. articles.title: I built an image-history manager for long Codex and Claude conversations
articles.summary: I was iterating on images with GPT in one long Codex task when the conversation started repeatedly reconnecting. In that task, requests carrying the accumulated image history had grown to about 44 MB. Starting a new conversation reduced the baggage, but separated me from the references, previous edits, and feedback I wanted to keep using. That led to Context Attachment Manager, an MIT-licensed local plugin for image-heavy conversations in Codex desktop and Claude Desktop's Code tab. GitHub repository · Install instructions Keep the conversation; retrieve images when needed With Auto-select enabled, images from earlier turns can be left out of later requests. When the model needs to inspect an earlier image, it can fetch that image back by its ID. For a character reference or another image that should always remain visible, pin it to send every turn.
